title: A week later
topic: Your own health, fatigue and wellbeing
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in the Emergency Department. A week ago you were part of the team that tried to resuscitate a three-year-old who later died.

You keep replaying it, are sleeping badly, and feel anxious when a child is brought in. You haven't told anyone.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Talk to your educational supervisor about how you are feeling.
options.brief: Your supervisor can support you and adjust your work if needed.
options.detailed: Your reaction is understandable. Your supervisor can offer support, help you access more, and consider whether any adjustments would help.

options.text: Avoid seeing children in the department for a while.
options.detailed: This may feel protective, but avoidance can make anxiety worse, and isn't sustainable in ED.

options.text: Contact your GP or the trust's staff support service.
options.brief: Professional support can help with persistent distress.
options.detailed: Persistent symptoms a week later may benefit from professional support. It ranks second because your supervisor can also support you at work.

options.text: Ask whether a team debrief has been arranged.
options.brief: Debriefs help staff process difficult events together.
options.detailed: Others in the team may feel similarly. A debrief can help everyone. It ranks third because you need individual support too.

options.text: Keep going, as these feelings usually fade.
options.brief: They may, but persistent symptoms deserve support.
options.detailed: Many people recover with time, but you are a week on and still struggling. Ignoring it risks your health and work.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you recognise the effects of a traumatic event on you and seek support.
explanation.keyDetails: It's a week later and you're still affected. You haven't told anyone. It's affecting your work.
explanation.reasoning: [A] gets support at work, [C] gets professional support, and [D] gets team support. [B] avoids the problem, and [E] ignores it.
explanation.competing: The order of [B] and [E] is close. The key ranks ignoring it last because avoidance is at least an acknowledgement, while ignoring it leaves you unsupported.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, looking after your own health.
